record_reviews.summary: Darwin thanks Sedgwick for a kind note concerning Emma's case and says he cannot attend the Aberdeen meeting because of ill health (P1–4). The letter recalls Sedgwick's 1831 geological excursion, but its immediate subject is personal/administrative; no specific incoming prompt is identifiable beyond the missing note from Sedgwick.

record_reviews.summary: Darwin tells Sedgwick that Murray will send the Origin and acknowledges that its conclusions oppose Sedgwick's long-advocated position (P1). The letter is a deliberate pre-publication dispatch and does not establish that Sedgwick had received or read the book; the later 2548 is the identifiable response.
record_reviews.date_assessment: To Adam Sedgwick 11 November [1859]1Down Bromley Kent [Ilkley.]Nov. 11th.—
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: A scoped candidate 2548 is recorded below; no other prompt is identified.

record_reviews.summary: Sedgwick says the Origin arrived in the latter part of the previous week, was read through despite interruptions, and was finished on Tuesday (P1). He then gives a sustained critique: natural selection is a secondary consequence, final cause remains necessary, and Darwin overstates geological evidence (P2–5), ending in an affectionate but explicit disagreement (P6–7). This is a source-complete reply to 2525's book dispatch, with receipt and reading stated by Sedgwick.

Darwin answers Sedgwick's severe criticism, saying he expected it and has worked on the subject for over twenty years (P1). He defends the theory's explanatory reach, concedes possible overconfidence, and says truth must survive attacks (P1–2), then thanks Sedgwick for writing (P3). The November 26 date follows the November 24 critique; this is a reverse reply to 2548, not a new prompt for the book dispatch.

record_reviews.summary: Darwin asks Babington a carefully framed botanical question: whether botanists unconsciously record varieties more often in large or small genera, explicitly separating recording bias from actual variability (P1–4). He asks Babington for an independent answer after discussing Hooker's suggestion (P2–5). No earlier Babington prompt is preserved; the later 2231 directly answers these numbered questions.
record_reviews.date_assessment: To Charles Cardale Babington 22 February [1858]1Down Bromley KentFeb. 22d
record_reviews.unmatched_reason: No earlier Babington prompt is preserved; 2231 is a later incoming answer, recorded below.

record_reviews.summary: Babington says he initially saw no difference but now thinks varieties are more often recorded in larger genera because many-species genera prompt closer observation; a botanical friend instead expects new plants in small genera because those are neglected (P1–2). He asks Darwin to share the combined results (P3–4). This March 3 incoming source answers 2220's recording-bias question, while the friend's statement is reported third-party voice.
record_reviews.date_assessment: From C. C. Babington 3 March 1858St John’s College | Cambridge3 Mar. 1858

record_reviews.summary: Darwin thanks Babington for the careful answer and says it agrees with Hooker, Bentham and Watson (P1). He reports his tabulation of Floras and six volumes of De Candolle, then explains that the observed excess of varieties in large genera may be recording bias rather than real variability (P2). This March 4 outgoing letter is a direct scoped reply to 2231; its own account of other botanists and data must remain Darwin's voice.
record_reviews.date_assessment: To C. C. Babington 4 March [1858]1Down Bromley KentMarch 4th

record_reviews.summary: Sedgwick's September 4, 1831 letter answers Darwin's North Wales geological observations: it discusses madrepores, terebratulae, slate and trap relations, and gives a detailed route and rock assessment, including his uncertainty about the exact Lake Ogwen spot (P1–5). The source contains a separate diagram visual and a postscript promising further traverses; it is early geological correspondence, not current-period knowledge.

Sedgwick's September 18, 1831 source combines book advice for Darwin with an account of anticlinal structure in the Carnarvon chain and a labelled section diagram (P1–9), plus an invitation to write to Carnarvon (P10). Its XML date is exact and the diagram is part of the source, but this earlier incoming letter is contextual only.

Babington reports on Darwin's Australian, New Zealand and Tierra del Fuego water beetles, naming genera and species counts while admitting he has not examined them carefully and will complete descriptions after the vacation (P1–2). He proposes sending the account to the Entomological Society and distinguishes Hope's requested description from his broader work (P2). This 1837 response is historical context, not a prompt for 1858 letters.
record_reviews.date_assessment: From Charles Cardale Babington 1 July 1837St John’s Coll: CambridgeJuly 1. 1837.

record_reviews.summary: Darwin explains that the Geological Society Council declined to recommend Jukes formally, while he and Whewell would assist with a Newfoundland application and Darwin offers further help (P1–3). This is an institutional recommendation exchange, not scientific evidence for the later Sedgwick/Origin sequence.

record_reviews.summary: Babington identifies Darwin's buried Atriplex specimen as a variety of A. angustifolia, explains how rich mud or manure could produce its appearance, rejects A. hastata, and asks to see Henslow's A. patula specimens (P1–5). It is a concrete botanical determination from 1843 and an earlier response to Darwin's specimen inquiry, not current-period knowledge.

record_reviews.summary: Darwin acknowledges Sedgwick's discourse received after sending for parcels and says he plans to read its educational ideas while deciding on a school for his son (P1–5). The source is a personal acknowledgement of receipt and intended reading, not evidence that Sedgwick's discourse supplied a current scientific prompt.

record_reviews.summary: Babington's damaged June 1855 letter says he marked points on Darwin's paper, treats oxlip, cowslip and primrose as distinct species capable of hybridisation, and discusses cultivated 'calycantha' and flower-colour variation (P1–6). The missing passages and CD's separate pencil notes remain distinct; the uncertain date is a month range and this is contextual botanical evidence only.

Babington answers questions about Subularia flowering above water, cautiously recalling possible aerial flowers, and separately reports that a university catalogue entry for an anonymous pigeon book cannot be located after the class was broken up (P1–4). The two topics are separate and the November 1856 date is explicit; neither supplies a prompt for the current Babington exchange.

proposed_links.reason: Sedgwick explicitly says the Origin arrived, was read through and finished, then critiques natural selection and final cause. His receipt/reading follows Darwin's 11 November dispatch; scope is the book dispatch and resulting critique.
proposed_links.response_scope: 2548 P1–P7 to 2525 P1; no claim that every later argument answers the dispatch.

evidence.quote: I have told Murray to send you a copy of my book on the Origin of Species
So soon as I opened it I began to read it, & I finished it

proposed_links.reason: Darwin explicitly responds to Sedgwick's severe disapprobation and defends the theory after the November 24 critique. This is a reverse reply to the received critique, not a second response to the original dispatch.

evidence.quote: You could not possibly have paid me a more honourable compliment than in expressing freely your strong disapprobation of my Book.
I have read your book with more pain than pleasure.

proposed_links.reason: Babington answers Darwin's explicitly framed recording-bias question, giving his own view and reporting a botanical friend's alternative. Scope is the genus-size/variety-recording question only.

evidence.quote: Do you think that good Botanists in drawing up a local Flora
there is a greater tendency generally to note “varieties” in the larger genera rather than in the very small ones

proposed_links.reason: Darwin thanks Babington for the careful answer and reports how it changes his interpretation of his tabulated Floras. Scope is the answer and its implications for recording bias; other botanists remain reported voices.
